query: W melts near 3422 °C, whereas Cu boils near 2562 °C, so conventional induction or arc-plasma casting cannot readily yield a uniform W–Cu material. Phase separation and void formation can impair thermal transport. Filling a W skeleton with molten Cu or Cu powder can leave defects; spark-plasma sintering and mechanical alloying can produce finer, more uniform structures but can also leave voids; vapor-coated W powders have been sintered to achieve near-perfect contact between the constituents; and metal 3D printing has also been explored. Starting from W particles or connected W regions within a Cu matrix for heat transfer under irradiation in fusion-reactor joints, what single intervention could overcome these limitations while preserving mechanical durability? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts an outcome relative to a named existing fabrication baseline, defines the processing and service boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment and observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Employing a powder metallurgy route—specifically, mechanical alloying of W and Cu powders followed by rapid consolidation via spark plasma sintering (SPS)—will yield a uniform, nanostructured W–Cu composite with minimized voids and phase separation, thereby enhancing thermal transport and mechanical durability under fusion irradiation compared to conventional infiltration or melting‐based methods.
generation.material_initial_state: W particles or connected W regions within a Cu matrix produced by conventional methods (e.g., infiltration casting, spark-plasma sintering of preformed W skeletons)
generation.intervention: Utilize mechanical alloying (MA) of tungsten and copper powders, and then rapidly consolidate the MA powders using SPS at temperatures below the individual melting points to promote fine-scale mixing and interfacial bonding.
generation.conditions: Processing under a controlled atmosphere to avoid oxidation, with rapid heating and cooling rates during SPS to prevent grain coarsening; service conditions include high irradiation environments typical in fusion-reactor joints.
generation.structural_mediator: A nanostructured, homogeneous W–Cu interface with minimal interfacial voids and defects
generation.mechanism: Mechanical alloying imparts high energy to the powders, enabling atomic-level mixing and increasing contact between dissimilar elements, while SPS rapidly densifies the composite below melting temperatures. Together, these effects suppress phase separation and void formation, resulting in continuous interfaces that enhance both thermal conduction and mechanical stability under irradiation.
generation.predicted_outcome: The MA+SPS fabricated composite is expected to show reduced void content, improved thermal conductivity, and greater mechanical durability under irradiation when compared to composites formed by traditional molten-casting or infiltration techniques.
generation.baseline: Conventional fabrication routes such as filling a W skeleton with molten Cu, arc-plasma casting, or standard sintering methods from preformed powders, which often suffer from phase separation and void formation.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be most effective at temperatures below those that would induce significant grain growth/coarsening, and under irradiation conditions typical in fusion-reactor joint applications; beyond these limits, the benefits may diminish.
generation.uncertainty: While prior reports in high-entropy alloy fabrication via MA+SPS support the feasibility of achieving a uniform, defect-minimized microstructure, the exact magnitude of thermal and mechanical improvements in a W–Cu system under irradiation remains to be quantitatively determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set using the proposed MA+SPS process for W–Cu composite fabrication and a control set using a conventional fabrication method (e.g., infiltration or arc-plasma casting). Expose both sample sets to simulated fusion reactor irradiation and thermal cycling to replicate service conditions.
measurements: Void fraction and density (via microscopy and density measurements)
Mechanical property testing (e.g., hardness, compressive strength)
Microstructural characterization using SEM/TEM to assess homogeneity and interface quality
Assessment of irradiation-induced damage (e.g., using post-irradiation examination)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples produced via MA+SPS do not show a statistically significant reduction in void fraction, an improvement in thermal conductivity, and enhanced mechanical durability (as measured by strength and resistance to irradiation-induced degradation) relative to the conventional baseline, the hypothesis will be falsified.

Compared with the more frequently studied casting, sintering has a great economic advantage in saving materials and energy []. On the other hand, the element distribution in sintered alloys is usually more inhomogeneous than that of casted ones. One example is the Cr, Mn, and O enrichment in spark-plasma-sintered alloys []. The zones with specific element enrichment generally affect the mechanical properties and electrochemical stability. In addition, the impurities of carbon or oxygen from raw powders also play essential roles in the above properties. Therefore, the relationship between the specific microstructure, the mechanical properties, and the electrochemical stability of sintered alloys needs to be sufficiently clarified. The WxTaTiVCr high-entropy alloy with 32at.% of tungsten (W) and its derivative alloys with 42 to 90at.% of W with in-situ TiC were prepared via the mixing of elemental W, Ta, Ti, V and Cr powders followed by spark plasma sintering for the development of reduced-activation alloys for fusion plasma-facing materials. Characterization of the sintered samples revealed a BCC lattice and a multi-phase structure. The selected-area diffraction patterns confirmed the formation of TiC in the high-entropy alloy and its derivative alloys. It revealed the development of C15 (cubic) Laves phases as well in alloys with 71 to 90at.% W. A mechanical examination of the samples revealed a more than twofold improvement in the hardness and strength due to solid-solution strengthening and dispersion strengthening. This study explored the potential of powder metallurgy processing for the fabrication of a high-entropy alloy and other derived compositions with enhanced hardness and strength.

A possible way to solve the problem of manufacturing Co-Cr-Cu-Fe-Ni HEAs that would exhibit a combination of excellent mechanical properties is to form the non-cast types of microstructure using alternative technologies for their production (e.g., the methods based on powder metallurgy). It has been demonstrated in refs. [,,] that single-phase CoCrCuxFeNi alloys having a nanocrystalline microstructure can be manufactured employing mechanically alloyed (MA) powder mixtures as starting materials and consolidation methods such as hot pressing (HP) or spark plasma sintering (SPS). The advantages of this technology over casting are as follows. Mechanical alloying can be used to produce solid solutions from metal powders due to high-energy mechanical impacts (multiple collisions with grinding bodies in the milling jars) despite the limitations or even the complete absence of mutual solubility []. The HP and SPS methods are used to consolidate powder materials at temperatures below the melting point of the main components. Therefore, the nanocrystalline microstructure inherited from the MA powders is preserved.

chosen.approach: Powder metallurgy (MA + SPS) for high‐entropy alloy fabrication
